title: GOD CALLED IT WICKEDNESS: THE FORBIDDEN FAMILY RELATIONSHIP THAT LEVITICUS EXPOSED
paragraphs: GOD CALLED IT WICKEDNESS: THE FORBIDDEN FAMILY RELATIONSHIP THAT LEVITICUS EXPOSED

One man. One family. One boundary God refused to let anyone cross. But behind this disturbing command is a truth about sexual sin, broken trust, hidden shame, and the mercy of Jesus Christ that every generation desperately needs to hear.
What if the sin you keep calling a private matter is quietly destroying the people who trusted you most?
There are sins that happen in public.

And there are sins that happen behind locked doors, inside homes where everyone smiles at the dinner table, where family photographs still hang on the walls, and where the people being betrayed have no idea that something sacred has already been violated.
Sometimes the most devastating betrayal doesn't come from an enemy.
It comes from someone who was supposed to protect the family.
Someone who knew the boundaries.
Someone who understood the trust.
Someone who crossed the line anyway.
And thousands of years ago, God spoke into that darkness with a command so direct that it still makes modern readers uncomfortable.
A man was forbidden from having a sexual relationship with a woman and her daughter. The prohibition also extended to her granddaughter.
Listen carefully to the words of Leviticus 18:17 in the King James Version:

“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, neither shalt thou take her son's daughter, or her daughter's daughter, to uncover her nakedness; for they are her near kinswomen: it is wickedness.”
Read that again.
Not because the language is sensational.
But because God was protecting something that human desire has repeatedly tried to destroy.
The sanctity of family relationships.
The trust between generations.
The dignity of people who must never become objects of another person's sexual appetite.
And the boundaries that protect a household from becoming a place of betrayal.
Here is something important that many people miss when discussing this passage.

Leviticus 18:17 does not specifically name a wife's mother. It forbids sexual relations with a woman and her daughter or granddaughter. The direct prohibition involving a man's mother-in-law appears in Leviticus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 27:23.
That distinction matters.
Because if we are going to speak in God's name, we must handle God's Word faithfully.
We do not need to exaggerate Scripture to make it powerful.
Its truth is already powerful enough.
And when we examine the original Hebrew, the message becomes even more sobering.
The expression translated “uncover the nakedness” comes from the Hebrew phrase לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה — legalot ervah.
In this legal context, it is a Hebrew expression referring to prohibited sexual relations.
It is not simply about accidentally seeing someone unclothed.
The passage concerns sexual conduct and forbidden family relationships.
And near the end of the verse appears another striking Hebrew expression:
זִמָּה הִוא — zimmah hi.
“It is wickedness.”
The Hebrew noun zimmah can describe a morally reprehensible act or scheme. Here, it condemns the sexual violation of the family boundary described in the passage.
God was not merely issuing an arbitrary social preference.
He was identifying behavior that corrupts the relationships a family depends upon.
And the context makes this even clearer.
In Leviticus 18:6, God establishes the broader principle:
“None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD.”
Notice how the command ends.
“I am the LORD.”
Not, “This is merely how your ancestors lived.”
Not, “This is only a matter of personal taste.”
Not, “Follow whatever your desires tell you.”
God grounds His instruction in His own authority.
The One who created human beings also has the right to establish moral boundaries for human relationships.
And this is where the passage becomes painfully relevant.
Because we live in a world where people often confuse desire with permission.
Where attraction is treated as justification.
Where secrecy is mistaken for safety.
Where someone can tell themselves that an action is harmless simply because nobody has discovered it.
But secrecy does not make betrayal innocent.
And the absence of witnesses does not mean the absence of consequences.
Imagine a family gathering.
The children are laughing.
The food is being prepared.
A husband sits beside his wife.
Her mother is nearby, helping with the meal.
There is nothing inappropriate about the scene. It is ordinary family life.
But imagine that the husband begins entertaining sexual thoughts about his wife's mother.
He knows the relationship.
He knows the trust.
He knows what it would mean if he pursued those desires.
Yet instead of turning away, he begins feeding the fantasy.
A conversation becomes flirtation.
Flirtation becomes secrecy.
Secrecy becomes rationalization.
And eventually, he faces a decision that could devastate his marriage and fracture an entire family.
This is an illustration, not a story recorded in Leviticus.
But the moral danger is real.
And it reveals why God's boundaries are not enemies of love.
They are meant to protect the relationships that love has a responsibility to honor.
A mother-in-law is not another romantic possibility for a married man.
A daughter is not a sexual alternative to her mother.
A granddaughter is not someone whose family connection can be ignored when desire appears.
These relationships carry obligations that sexual exploitation and betrayal would violate.
And Scripture refuses to treat those obligations as disposable.
Now consider something even more disturbing.
The damage from such wrongdoing would rarely stop with the two people involved.
Think about the wife.
The daughter.
The grandchildren.
The family members who suddenly discover that relationships they believed were safe have been violated.
The people who must live with questions they never wanted to ask.
Was any of it real?
How long was this happening?
Who knew?
Who lied?
Can I trust anyone again?
Sexual betrayal can leave consequences that last long after the secret is exposed.
And when coercion, manipulation, or abuse is involved, the harm can be even more severe.
God's command is not permission to shame those who have been harmed.
The responsibility for abuse belongs to the person who commits it.
A victim is not guilty because someone violated a boundary against them.
And genuine repentance never requires a victim to remain in danger, surrender appropriate boundaries, or conceal wrongdoing.
That is worth saying clearly because some people have used religious language to protect reputations while ignoring wounded people.
But biblical holiness is not a costume worn to hide corruption.
It is a call to walk in truth before God.
And this is where the story becomes more than an ancient prohibition.
Because the question is no longer simply whether a man should pursue his wife's mother.
The question becomes:
What are you allowing into your heart that you already know has no rightful place there?
Maybe you have never faced the particular temptation described in Leviticus.
But perhaps there is a conversation you keep deleting.
A relationship you keep explaining away.
A private attachment that has become emotionally intimate in ways you would never openly acknowledge.
A boundary you have been moving little by little because crossing it all at once would have frightened your conscience.
Or perhaps your struggle has nothing to do with sexual temptation.
Maybe it is dishonesty.
Bitterness.
Envy.
A hidden addiction.
A habit you have defended for years.
Something that has slowly taken control of your decisions while you continue telling everyone that you are fine.
The specific sin may be different.
But the spiritual danger is familiar.
We begin by making room for what we should resist.
Then we become accustomed to what once troubled us.
And eventually, we risk calling normal what God has called us to turn away from.
The Bible warns us about this progression.
James 1:14–15 says:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
Notice the movement.
Desire.
Enticement.
Sin.
Death.
James does not teach that every unwanted temptation makes someone guilty of having committed the act.
Temptation and chosen sin are not identical.
But he does warn that when sinful desire is embraced and allowed to govern our actions, it can produce devastating consequences.
And Jesus takes this warning deeper.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He teaches:

“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Jesus was not saying that an involuntary thought is the same as physically committing adultery.
He was exposing the moral seriousness of deliberately cultivating lust.
He was showing that obedience is not merely about avoiding an outward act while privately nurturing the desire to commit it.
God cares about what happens inside us.
The thoughts we entertain.
The intentions we protect.
The choices we make when nobody else can see.
And that truth can be uncomfortable.
Because a person may appear faithful while inwardly becoming consumed by unfaithfulness.
A person may know the language of holiness while repeatedly negotiating with temptation.
A person may attend church, sing worship songs, and quote Bible verses while refusing to confront a hidden pattern of sin.
But here is where we must be careful.
The purpose of exposing sin is not to convince people that they are beyond redemption.
It is to bring what is hidden into the light so that repentance, truth, and transformation become possible.
And no one demonstrates that purpose more clearly than Jesus Christ.
Think about the woman brought before Him in John 8.
She was publicly accused of adultery.
The crowd stood ready to condemn her.
Her shame was no longer private.
Her situation had become a public spectacle.
And Jesus refused to participate in the crowd's hypocrisy.
He confronted the accusers.
Then, when they had gone, He spoke to the woman.
John 8:11 records His words:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Do not miss either half of that statement.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
Mercy.
“Go, and sin no more.”
A call to repentance.
Jesus did not celebrate adultery.
He did not pretend sin was harmless.
He did not tell the woman that holiness no longer mattered.
But neither did He join a crowd eager to destroy her.
His response revealed a mercy that refused to abandon truth.
And a truth that did not extinguish mercy.
That is the Gospel we desperately need.
Not a message that excuses every desire.
Not a message that humiliates every sinner.
But the good news that Jesus Christ came to save sinners and transform lives.
Consider what Paul wrote to the Corinthians.
In 1 Corinthians 6:9–10, he warns that those who persist in unrighteousness must not presume upon the kingdom of God.
His list includes sexual immorality and other serious sins.
But then comes one of the most beautiful sentences in the New Testament.
1 Corinthians 6:11:
“And such were some of you.”
Pause there.
Were.
Not because their past had never happened.
Not because their actions had no consequences.
Not because everyone they harmed had automatically recovered.
But because their former sins no longer defined their standing before God in Christ.
Paul continues:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
Look at those words.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
The Greek word translated “washed” is ἀπελούσασθε — apelousasthe.
It points to washing or cleansing.
The word translated “sanctified” is ἡγιάσθητε — hēgiasthēte.
It speaks of being made holy or set apart.
And “justified” translates ἐδικαιώθητε — edikaiōthēte.
It refers to being declared righteous or put into right standing.
Paul is describing what God has done for believers through Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit.
He is not claiming that conversion erases every earthly consequence.
He is proclaiming that sin does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that.
Because you have been carrying something.
Maybe a choice you made years ago.
Maybe a relationship that crossed a boundary.
Maybe a betrayal you deeply regret.
Maybe a past you have tried to bury because you are terrified of what people would think if they knew.
You have learned how to smile.
How to function.
How to keep going.
But sometimes, when everything becomes quiet, the memories return.
And you wonder whether God could still receive someone like you.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity had managed to keep itself clean. He came because sinners needed a Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had repaired every mistake.
Not after we had earned forgiveness.
Not after we had finally become impressive enough to deserve divine attention.
Christ died for sinners.
And that includes people whose sins have left them deeply ashamed.
But grace is not permission to keep harming others.
Grace calls us out of darkness.
If you have betrayed someone, repentance means more than feeling guilty.
It means turning away from the wrongdoing.
Ending the sinful conduct.
Refusing to keep manipulating the truth.
Accepting accountability.
And, where possible and appropriate, taking responsible steps to address the harm without demanding immediate forgiveness or restored trust.
If abuse or criminal conduct has occurred, protecting those at risk and involving appropriate authorities must not be replaced by private religious assurances.
Forgiveness does not eliminate the need for justice.
And reconciliation cannot be forced.
This is not a contradiction of grace.
It is part of taking sin and the dignity of other people seriously.
Now return to Leviticus.
Why would God speak so directly about relationships that many people would rather never discuss?
Because the Lord was teaching His people that sexuality was not a lawless territory where appetite alone determined what was right.
In Leviticus 18:3–5, Israel is instructed not to imitate the practices of Egypt or Canaan, but to walk according to God's statutes.
The chapter establishes boundaries around sexual relationships as part of Israel's covenant life.
Christians must read these commands in their historical and covenantal context, rather than treating every feature of Israel's ancient civil law as directly applicable today.
Yet the New Testament continues to condemn sexual immorality and calls believers to honor marriage, holiness, and the dignity of others.
Hebrews 13:4 declares:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
And 1 Thessalonians 4:3 says:
“For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication.”
The biblical vision is not that human sexuality is inherently dirty.
It is that sexuality matters.
It has moral significance.
And its misuse can wound people in profoundly personal ways.
God's boundaries are not an expression of contempt for human beings.
They reflect His concern for how human beings treat one another.
But perhaps the most challenging question is not whether we agree with the prohibition.
Perhaps it is whether we are willing to let Scripture correct us when our desires disagree with it.
Because everyone enjoys the comforting passages.
The promises of peace.
The assurance of forgiveness.
The beautiful declarations of God's love.
And rightly so.
Those truths are precious.
But what happens when the Bible confronts a relationship we do not want to surrender?
A behavior we do not want to stop?
A secret we do not want exposed?
Will we still listen?
Will we still trust the God whose mercy we gladly receive?
Or will we begin editing His Word to protect what we want?
Jesus said in John 14:15:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.”
That is not a declaration that obedience purchases salvation.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward earned through moral perfection.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
But genuine faith does not regard obedience as meaningless.
Ephesians 2:10 goes on to say that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves us.
And the same grace begins reshaping how we live.
Sometimes that transformation is painful.
Because surrender means letting go of things we have grown attached to.
It means admitting that a desire can be powerful and still be wrong.
It means recognizing that love is not always demonstrated by saying yes.
Sometimes love says no.
No to betrayal.
No to exploitation.
No to the fantasy that another person's dignity is less important than our gratification.
No to the lie that hidden wrongdoing becomes acceptable when it feels emotionally satisfying.
And yes to truth.
Yes to repentance.
Yes to accountability.
Yes to the freedom of living without having to build an entire life around protecting a secret.
There is a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from hiding.
The constant calculations.
The fear of being discovered.
The effort of maintaining appearances.
The way a guilty conscience can turn ordinary conversations into moments of anxiety.
And there is another kind of pain carried by those who have been betrayed.
The confusion.
The grief.
The anger.
The struggle to trust again.
Some people reading this are not the ones who crossed the boundary.
They are the ones who suffered because somebody else did.
If that is you, hear this clearly.
You are not responsible for another person's decision to violate your trust.
You do not have to minimize the harm to prove that you are a Christian.
You do not have to pretend you are healed when you are still hurting.
And you do not have to allow someone continued access to your life simply because they claim to have repented.
God's grace is real.
So is the need for safety, wisdom, support, and time.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
The Lord sees the brokenhearted.
He does not despise their pain.
And the Gospel offers hope to both the repentant sinner and the wounded person, without confusing their responsibilities or minimizing what happened.
This is why the cross of Jesus Christ stands at the center of everything we teach at Gospel Warrior.
At Calvary, sin was not dismissed as a small inconvenience.
Its seriousness was revealed in the suffering and death of the Savior.
Yet God's love was also revealed there.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
His resurrection declares that death does not have the final victory.
And through Him, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who repent and believe.
That is not merely an inspirational message.
It is the heart of the Christian Gospel.
And it changes how we read a disturbing passage like Leviticus 18:17.
We no longer read it merely to be shocked by the sins people are capable of committing.
We read it with reverence for the God who establishes moral boundaries.
With compassion for those harmed when those boundaries are violated.
With humility about our own vulnerability to temptation.
And with gratitude that Jesus Christ is able to save and transform sinners.
Perhaps today is the day you stop defending something that has been damaging your soul.
Perhaps it is time to end a secret relationship.
To seek wise pastoral counsel.
To speak truthfully.
To pursue professional help where needed.
To confess to God what you have spent years trying to justify.
Or perhaps today is the day you stop blaming yourself for someone else's betrayal and begin seeking the care and support you deserve.
Whatever your circumstances, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The Holy Spirit's work is not to lead us into endless despair.
He directs us toward Christ, truth, repentance, and the life that follows.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no need to pretend before a God who already knows the truth.
And there is no need to believe that the worst chapter of your life must be the last.
From scandal to grace is not the story of sin becoming harmless. It is the story of Jesus Christ being powerful enough to redeem sinners without ever calling evil good.
And if these words have confronted something in your heart, do not rush past that moment.
Pray.
Examine yourself before the Lord.
You might simply write, “Lord, teach me to honor Your boundaries.”
You do not need to disclose private sexual details, name anyone who harmed you, or reveal something that would place you or another person at risk.
Sometimes the most meaningful confession begins quietly before God.
And sometimes a simple request for prayer reminds someone else that they are not alone in their struggle.
There is another reason I hope you will not keep this article to yourself.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who may be wrestling with a secret temptation.
Someone whose marriage is under strain.
Someone who has been betrayed.
Someone who believes their past has made them unreachable by grace.
You may not know who they are.
And you do not need to know.
If a particular friend comes to mind, consider tagging them privately and thoughtfully, without implying that they are guilty of the sins discussed here.
Not because following a page makes someone a Christian.
But because regular exposure to Scripture, faithful teaching, encouragement, and Christ-centered discipleship can help people keep returning to the truth.
Not because every sentence will be easy to read.
But because some truths become especially important when temptation returns, when conscience grows quiet, or when someone you love needs encouragement to choose what is right.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, grow in your faith, or return to Jesus during a difficult season, I want to invite you into something deeper.

Our mission is to continue sharing the Gospel, teaching biblical truth, encouraging repentance, helping wounded people discover hope in Christ, and providing discipleship resources to those who are hungry for God's Word.
We want those resources to continue reaching people.
And we want to keep expanding the work.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
Not because financial support proves the strength of your faith.
But because generosity, when freely offered for a worthy purpose, can help sustain work that points people toward Jesus Christ.
Those products can be meaningful reminders of faith and opportunities to encourage others, but the heart of this invitation is not merchandise.
It is the Gospel.
It is Scripture.
It is the hope that someone who feels lost today may encounter the truth of Jesus Christ tomorrow.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And no one has to pay to come to Jesus.
We simply want to keep making Christ known.
Because at the end of the day, this article is not really about an ancient prohibition that makes modern people uncomfortable.
It is about the God who sees what happens behind closed doors.
The God who cares when families are betrayed.
The God who commands holiness because people matter.
The God who calls sinners to repentance.
And the God who sent His Son to redeem those who could never save themselves.
Maybe you began reading because the title shocked you.
Maybe you stayed because the Scripture challenged you.
Maybe something in these words reminded you of a wound, a regret, or a decision you have been avoiding.
But I pray you leave remembering something far greater than the scandal.
Jesus Christ is still calling people out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
He is still forgiving repentant sinners.
Still teaching His people to walk in holiness.
Still bringing hope to wounded hearts.
Still giving grace to those who come to Him in faith.
And still proving that the darkest truth about a person's past does not have to be the final truth about their future.
Not what someone else needs to repent of.
Not whose life this article reminds you of.
Not which person you think should read it.
Ask yourself:
Lord Jesus, what are You calling me to surrender, and will I trust You enough to obey?
Because the most dangerous secret is not always the one other people might discover.
Sometimes it is the one we keep defending even after God's Word has exposed it.
And the most beautiful turning point is not when we finally convince the world that we are good.
It is when we stop hiding from the Savior who already knows the truth and still calls us to come to Him.
The door you have been afraid to open may be the very place where repentance begins and the healing grace of Jesus Christ meets you.
